Let a small verifier, parser, harness, compiler route, registry contract or
kernel decide what is trusted, in place of a broad written account of why a
result looks right. The code that produces results may be large; the code that
decides should be small enough for a person to read and rerun.
nodes.title: Concentrate trust in small checkers

nodes.plain: Permission to change something comes from the referenced proof, policy, result record and rollback evidence, each opened and checked, together with the current state of the repository. A credential, a role name, administrator wording or a phrase such as "trusted session" is never enough on its own to authorize a change.

analogy.boundary: The bank picture covers only the gap between holding a credential and being cleared to act; it leaves out the specific permissions, rules and side-effect records weighed at decision time.

maps.analogy: simply having the card number
maps.doctrine: a standing credential or role name, which carries no permission alone

maps.analogy: the bank deciding each payment against this account, now
maps.doctrine: permission worked out for each action from policy and current state

analogy.text: Knowing someone's card number does not move money. For each payment the bank checks this card, this amount and the current account before it lets the transfer through.

reader.counterexample: A change goes ahead because the caller holds a valid admin credential, and nothing checks that credential against the specific effect, the policy or the current state.
reader.does_not_prove: These components show how permission is worked out for the effects they handle, and say nothing about effects that never pass through them.

example.text: The tool-authority replay ties each tool effect to a declared scope and approval and rejects a scope that is too broad or a side effect nobody approved, so a tool being callable gives it no extra reach.

reader.governs: Whether an effect or change may go ahead.
reader.plain: Holding a credential, having a role name or being in a 'trusted' session gives no permission to change anything by itself. Permission is worked out again for each action, from the rules and the current situation.
reader.potential_misread: That a valid credential is enough to act, when the credential is one input and the change still has to be cleared for that exact action against the current state.
reader.refuses: Treating a standing credential, role name, admin wording, trusted session or an available tool as permission on its own.
reader.requires: Authorization worked out from looked-up proof, policy and current state, with each tool effect limited to its declared identity, scope, approval and side-effect records.
reader.why_it_matters: A component holding broad power cannot be talked into using it for someone else, because each action needs its own permission.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-3.
Obligation grounding: AX-3.O1.authorization_is_derived, AX-3.O2.standing_credential_insufficient, AX-3.O3.tool_effects_require_declared_scope.

Permission to change something comes from the referenced proof, policy, result
record and rollback evidence, each opened and checked, together with the current
state of the repository. A credential, a role name, administrator wording or a
phrase such as "trusted session" is never enough on its own to authorize a
change.
nodes.title: Possession is not permission

nodes.plain: A saved result, command output, source import or work-landing attempt that may be reused must record a hash of the exact content it was computed from. Any change to the source bytes, to uncommitted files in its scope, to the parent commit or to the fixture input means it has to be recomputed.

analogy.boundary: The serial number covers only matching the exact item; it leaves out other kinds of change the rule watches for, such as edited files or a moved parent commit.

maps.analogy: the warranty holds only while the serial number matches the unit
maps.doctrine: reuse only when the saved content tag matches the current inputs

maps.analogy: trusting the model name on the box instead of the serial number
maps.doctrine: a matching name or label allowing reuse

analogy.text: A warranty covers the exact unit whose serial number is on the claim. If a part with a different serial number was swapped in, the matching model name on the box does not carry the warranty over.

reader.counterexample: A resumed landing attempt reuses an earlier result because the task name matches, although the parent commit and the files in scope have changed.
reader.does_not_prove: These reuse paths record their inputs, and one known case where the recorded input and the current input can disagree is still open.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings public material in with a manifest and a hash for each file, so when the source bytes change the imported copy is recomputed instead of being reused under the same name.

reader.governs: The point where an earlier result is about to be reused instead of recomputed.
reader.plain: A saved result can be reused only if it is tagged with the exact inputs it was made from and those inputs still match. If the inputs have changed, the work has to be redone, whatever the name or label says.
reader.potential_misread: That a matching name or path means the cached answer is still good, when only a match on the content it was computed from allows reuse.
reader.refuses: Serving a cached result looked up by name, path or label after the content behind it has changed.
reader.requires: A hash of the input content saved with the result, reuse only when that hash still matches, and a recompute or refusal as soon as the source, files in scope, parent commit or fixture input change.
reader.why_it_matters: A stale or tampered result cannot be served as fresh just because its name or path still looks familiar.

nodes.statement:

Obligation grounding: AX-4.O1.content_basis_digest_declared, AX-4.O2.equal_basis_permits_reuse, AX-4.O3.digest_drift_forces_recompute, AX-4.O4.freshness_basis_mismatch_materialized.

be reused must record a hash of the exact content it was computed from. Any
change to the source bytes, to uncommitted files in its scope, to the parent
commit or to the fixture input means it has to be recomputed.
nodes.title: Cache by content, not by name

nodes.plain: A missing piece of evidence, policy file, source digest, secret scan, negative case or self-scan of a result record blocks the result or lowers its status. A generated summary further downstream can explain why something passed, and it can never turn a blocked source into a pass.

analogy.boundary: The building picture covers why an uninspected part holds the whole back; a complete set of sign-offs still does not mean nothing was missed.

maps.analogy: the building is fit only if every trade passes, and the worst result decides
maps.doctrine: a combined status takes the lowest status of its parts

maps.analogy: a trade with no inspection on file counts as failed
maps.doctrine: a part with no evidence counts as blocked

maps.analogy: a later walk-through can downgrade the building and needs a fresh passing inspection to approve it
maps.doctrine: a later step may lower a status and needs new evidence to raise it

analogy.text: A building cannot be signed off for use until wiring, plumbing and fire safety have all passed. If the fire inspection never happened, the building stays unfit, and a later walk-through can find a new fault but cannot approve it alone.

reader.counterexample: A status board shows a component as green because no scan reported a problem, counting a check that never ran as a pass.
reader.does_not_prove: Failing closed decides what happens when evidence is missing; whether the parts that have evidence are correct is a separate question.

example.text: The formal-math readiness gate takes the lowest status among its inputs, so when the corpus or a required check is missing it reports blocked, and a later summary cannot change that to passing.

reader.governs: How a combined status is built from its parts when some evidence is missing.
reader.plain: A combined result is only as sound as its weakest part. If one part has no evidence behind it, the whole counts as not ready. A later step can downgrade that verdict, and raising it takes fresh work.
reader.potential_misread: That an unchecked part is harmless and can count as a pass, or that a summary page can promote something that was blocked underneath it.
reader.refuses: A silent default pass, where missing evidence, a skipped scan or a summary page turns a blocked part green.
reader.requires: Taking the lowest status among the parts, treating any part with no evidence as blocked, and requiring new evidence before a later step raises a status.
reader.why_it_matters: A missing check or skipped scan cannot quietly count as approval.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-5.
Obligation grounding: AX-5.O1.composite_status_meets_parts, AX-5.O2.no_evidence_defaults_blocked, AX-5.O3.authority_cannot_raise_without_derivation.

A missing piece of evidence, policy file, source digest, secret scan, negative
case or self-scan of a result record blocks the result or lowers its status. A
generated summary further downstream can explain why something passed, and it
can never turn a blocked source into a pass.
nodes.title: Status fails closed

nodes.plain: A coverage report names the domains it declared and the gaps it found inside them. Anything outside those domains stays unknown, and the report must never describe it as safe, complete, exhausted or irrelevant.

analogy.boundary: The catalogue picture covers only what silence outside the indexed shelves means, and says nothing about what the unindexed shelves hold.

maps.analogy: the catalogue speaks only for the shelves it lists as indexed
maps.doctrine: coverage holds only over a declared finite area

maps.analogy: a title missing from the catalogue may sit on a shelf nobody has indexed
maps.doctrine: items outside the area are unknown

maps.analogy: an empty search means this catalogue did not find the book, and the book may still exist
maps.doctrine: no finding is no evidence of safety or completeness

analogy.text: A library catalogue lists the shelves that have been indexed. A book missing from the catalogue may sit on a shelf nobody has indexed yet, so the catalogue's silence means unchecked.

reader.counterexample: A report scans a handful of components, finds nothing, and marks the whole area clear, as if the parts it never looked at had been checked.
reader.does_not_prove: Marking the unchecked area unknown keeps the report honest about its reach, and the gap itself stays open.

example.text: The self-ignorance coverage ledger records what was checked, lists the gaps it found as open items, and keeps a test case that fails when missing coverage is reported as a clean result.

reader.governs: How a report describes what it covered and what it left unexamined.
reader.plain: A coverage report can only speak about the area it actually checked, and it has to name that area and the gaps it found. Anything outside the area is unknown.
reader.potential_misread: That a report with no problems means the unchecked area is clear, complete or safe, when it is only unexamined.
reader.refuses: Turning the absence of a finding into a statement that the unchecked area is safe, complete, exhausted or irrelevant.
reader.requires: Naming the declared finite area and the gaps found in it, and marking everything outside that area as unknown.
reader.why_it_matters: A tidy report with no findings cannot be read as everything is fine when nothing outside its area was looked at.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-6.
Obligation grounding: AX-6.O1.closed_world_domain_declared, AX-6.O2.absence_not_negation, AX-6.O3.fact_claims_cite_loci_and_dag.

A coverage report names the domains it declared and the gaps it found inside
them. Anything outside those domains stays unknown, and the report must never
describe it as safe, complete, exhausted or irrelevant.
nodes.title: Track known unknowns without claiming the unknown is mapped

nodes.plain: When a precondition fails, return a refusal that gives the reason. Never emit a meaningless statistic, a proof status, a safety verdict or a public-readiness status just to keep a pipeline green.

analogy.boundary: The pharmacy picture covers withholding an unfounded answer; it does not say whether the original request was valid.

maps.analogy: the pharmacist dispenses only a complete, valid prescription
maps.doctrine: an Ok result only when the precondition holds

maps.analogy: an incomplete prescription comes back with the missing detail noted on it
maps.doctrine: a failed precondition returns a refusal with its reason and evidence

maps.analogy: the pharmacist does not invent a dose to avoid sending the patient away empty-handed
maps.doctrine: no meaningless value just to keep the run green

analogy.text: A pharmacist missing a required detail on a prescription hands it back with the reason written on it, instead of guessing a dose to send the patient away with a filled bottle.

reader.counterexample: A readiness gate reports a corpus as available and shows green while the library it needs is missing.
reader.does_not_prove: A refusal records that an answer was withheld and why; whether the refusal itself was correct is a separate question.

example.text: The finance forecast evaluation spine returns a typed refusal when the forecast horizon reaches or exceeds the sample size, or when the statistics library is unavailable, instead of reporting a loss difference the data cannot support.

reader.governs: What a computation returns when it cannot run properly.
reader.plain: When a step cannot be done properly because something it needs is missing, it should hand back a clear refusal that says why, instead of a made-up answer that makes the work look finished.
reader.potential_misread: That some number is always better than none, even when nothing supports that number.
reader.refuses: Producing a meaningless statistic, proof verdict, safety verdict or readiness status to keep the run green when the inputs do not support one.
reader.requires: An Ok result only when the declared precondition holds, and otherwise a refusal with a reason and evidence.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a system from reporting a forecast past its data, or a ready flag while a needed part is missing, just to avoid showing red.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-7.
Obligation grounding: AX-7.O1.ok_under_precondition, AX-7.O2.refusal_carries_reason_evidence, AX-7.O3.absent_library_refuses_not_overclaims.

When a precondition fails, return a refusal that gives the reason. Never emit a
meaningless statistic, a proof status, a safety verdict or a public-readiness
status just to keep a pipeline green.
nodes.title: Refuse inadmissible computations with typed reasons

nodes.plain: Every piece of data that moves out of the private source system, a fixture, a result record, public copy, a provider's response format or material stored next to the private root must carry a label saying where it came from and how strongly it may be claimed. If the flow is only declared, or labelled only at its end, say so.

analogy.boundary: The parcel picture covers only the difference between a label added at the end and a record carried all the way; an intact seal still says nothing about whether the contents are right.

maps.analogy: the parcel carries its custody log through every handoff
maps.doctrine: a value carries its origin class across each boundary

maps.analogy: the tamper seal is applied when packed and stays intact
maps.doctrine: the usage limit travels with the value from the start

maps.analogy: a sticker added at the last dock is logged as a late sticker
maps.doctrine: a label added only at the destination is recorded as such

analogy.text: A parcel carries a custody log and a tamper seal applied where it was packed. If a clean sticker was added at the last loading dock instead, the log has to say so.

reader.counterexample: A public page prints a value copied from a source next to private files because the final copy step looked clean, with no origin record carried across the copy.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching labelled flows at named boundaries covers those boundaries only, and full tracking across every path is a recorded open gap.

example.text: The prompt-injection replay keeps the information-flow policy attached to the data, so untrusted instructions arriving at a tool call are caught at that boundary even though they reached a trusted endpoint.

reader.governs: Every boundary a value crosses on its way from imported source to a public or privileged destination.
reader.plain: A value carries a record of where it came from and how far it may be used, and that record travels with it through every handoff. If something was only labelled clean at the final step, that has to be written down.
reader.potential_misread: That a clean label at the destination is enough, whether or not it travelled with the value through the earlier boundaries.
reader.refuses: Taking a clean label at the destination as evidence when it was added there and never travelled with the value.
reader.requires: An origin class and a usage limit carried with the value across each crossing, and a note whenever a flow is only declared or labelled at the destination.
reader.why_it_matters: A clean-looking final copy can still be treated as unchecked, so trust depends on where a value came from.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-8.
Obligation grounding: AX-8.O1.label_propagation, AX-8.O2.sink_policy, AX-8.O3.lying_endpoint_rejected.

Every piece of data that moves out of the private source system, a fixture, a
result record, public copy, a provider's response format or material stored next
to the private root must carry a label saying where it came from and how
strongly it may be claimed. If the flow is only declared, or labelled only at
its end, say so.
nodes.title: Preserve provenance across every boundary

nodes.plain: Writes, release steps, releasing a claim on a path, source imports and anything that can be rolled back need evidence that their steps ran in order as one transaction. Release a lock only after the durable records are written, recompute after the release, and block a change whose parent commit is stale or whose path someone else has claimed.

analogy.boundary: The transfer picture covers one transaction only; one clean transfer tells you nothing about the rest of the bank.

maps.analogy: the transfer being treated as sent
maps.doctrine: the effect being treated as done

maps.analogy: the entry in the bank's ledger
maps.doctrine: the lasting ordered record

maps.analogy: a reversal path, or a stated point after which it cannot be pulled back
maps.doctrine: a way to undo it, or a declared point of no return

maps.analogy: confirming the balance is still the one the clerk started from
maps.doctrine: compare-and-swap on the expected parent

maps.analogy: no second clerk touching the same account at the same moment
maps.doctrine: one writer holding the path

analogy.text: A bank transfer counts as sent once the bank writes it into its ledger, attaches a way to reverse it, and confirms no other clerk changed the same account at the same moment from an out-of-date balance.

reader.counterexample: A release step reports success after taking a lock and before writing the lasting record, so a crash in between leaves an effect that looks done with nothing to recompute or undo.
reader.does_not_prove: Guarding one transaction on one path says nothing about effects that never went through that guard.

example.text: The mission transaction work spine marks a multi-step change done only after the lasting record is written, recomputes once the lock is released, and blocks a stale parent or a conflict on the same path, so a half-applied write cannot be reported as complete.

reader.governs: The point where an operation is about to be treated as done.
reader.plain: An action counts as done only when there is a permanent record of it, a way to undo it or a stated point of no return, and a check that nobody else changed the same thing at the same time from outdated information. Running without errors is not enough.
reader.potential_misread: That an operation which reported success must be fully done, when the risky moment is the gap where a lock is released before the permanent record exists.
reader.refuses: Counting an operation as done when the lock was released before the record was written, the parent is stale, or a second writer is on the same path.
reader.requires: An ordered lasting record, a way to undo it or a declared irreversible point, a compare-and-swap on the expected parent, and one writer holding the path.
reader.why_it_matters: A step that crashes between starting and finishing could otherwise look complete while leaving a half-done change nobody can recompute or undo.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-9.
Obligation grounding: AX-9.O1.effect_boundary_declared, AX-9.O2.cas_parent_enforced, AX-9.O3.single_writer_claim_constraint.

Writes, release steps, releasing a claim on a path, source imports and anything
that can be rolled back need evidence that their steps ran in order as one
transaction. Release a lock only after the durable records are written,
recompute after the release, and block a change whose parent commit is stale or
whose path someone else has claimed.
nodes.title: Do not land effects without compensation

nodes.plain: Counts, "current" states, live route totals, CI minimums, body-import minimums and readiness signals must say how they can be recomputed. If they cannot be recomputed, leave them out of lasting prose or mark them as snapshots with a date.

analogy.boundary: The board covers why a changing value needs a timestamp and a live source; a refresh time on its own does not mean the value is correct now.

maps.analogy: the departure time shown for a train
maps.doctrine: a live count or readiness signal

maps.analogy: the 'last updated' stamp on the board
maps.doctrine: the read time carried with the value

maps.analogy: the board's link to the live timetable feed
maps.doctrine: the route that recomputes it from its source

maps.analogy: treating a time painted on the wall as an old notice
maps.doctrine: marking an unsupported value as a dated snapshot

analogy.text: A train departure board shows when it last refreshed and updates from the live feed. A time painted on the wall stops being reliable as soon as the timetable changes.

reader.counterexample: A page states "47 components" as a flat fact, with no read time and no way to recount, and the number stays the same after more components are added.
reader.does_not_prove: A recompute route lets a reader check the value; it does not mean anyone has recomputed it since it was written.

example.text: The doctrine fact-claim audit checks that public fact rows state the expected count, point at the live code they were read from and cite only facts in the fixture graph, and it blocks a changing number that has no way to be recomputed.

reader.governs: When a live reading may appear in lasting text.
reader.plain: A number about something that keeps changing, like a current count or a readiness status, may sit in a lasting document only if it says when it was read and how to work it out again. Otherwise mark it as a dated snapshot.
reader.potential_misread: That a confident number in a document is current because it sounds definite, when what matters is whether there is a way to recount it.
reader.refuses: A frozen live count or 'current' state written as a fact with no read time and no way to recompute it.
reader.requires: The read time, the source and a recompute route for every live count or readiness signal, or a dated-snapshot label when any is missing.
reader.why_it_matters: A frozen 'current' number drifts away from reality as the thing it counts changes, and readers keep trusting the old reading.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-10.
Obligation grounding: AX-10.O1.live_claim_carries_freshness_contract, AX-10.O2.stale_basis_requires_rederive, AX-10.O3.volatile_numeric_unbound_blocked.

Counts, "current" states, live route totals, CI minimums, body-import minimums
and readiness signals must say how they can be recomputed. If they cannot be
recomputed, leave them out of lasting prose or mark them as snapshots with a
date.
nodes.title: Bind volatile facts to refresh routes

nodes.plain: A doctrine document gains authority only when it passes the grammar, has its required fields, lists the result records it must produce and the statements of what it does not cover (its anti-claims), and has a validator that checks it. Until it has that executable contract, its prose can help a reader find their way and has no authority over the system.

analogy.boundary: The inspection picture covers only when a notice may govern; it says nothing about whether the room is well built or the code complete.

maps.analogy: the 'meets code' notice on the door
maps.doctrine: a doctrine document the system may treat as a rule

maps.analogy: passing the building inspection
maps.doctrine: passing the executable grammar

maps.analogy: the required sign-offs
maps.doctrine: the required fields and result-record obligations

maps.analogy: the notice saying what it does and does not certify
maps.doctrine: the stated limits of the rule

maps.analogy: a well-worded sign nobody inspected, which informs and authorizes nothing
maps.doctrine: prose that guides readers and governs nothing

analogy.text: A 'meets code' notice on a door controls who may enter only after an inspector checks the room against the building code with every required sign-off. A well-worded sign nobody inspected just informs people.

reader.counterexample: A persuasive markdown standard is used as the rule other components must meet, although nothing parses it against a grammar and it lists no records or limits.
reader.does_not_prove: Passing the grammar shows a document is well formed, and its content can still be wrong.

example.text: The executable doctrine grammar accepts a standard as a rule only when it parses under the grammar and carries its required fields, result-record obligations and stated limits, so a standard written only as prose stays a description.

reader.governs: When a doctrine document may act as a rule for other components.
reader.plain: A written rule can govern other parts of the system only after a program checks its form and finds its required parts and stated limits. Well-written words alone can guide a reader and nothing more.
reader.potential_misread: That clear, confident writing is enough to make something a binding rule, when passing the form check only means it is well formed.
reader.refuses: Giving unstructured prose the authority of a rule without the executable contract.
reader.requires: Passing the grammar, plus the required fields, result-record obligations and stated limits.
reader.why_it_matters: A persuasive paragraph cannot be treated as a rule other parts must obey before anything has checked it.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-11.
Obligation grounding: AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection.

A doctrine document gains authority only when it passes the grammar, has its
required fields, lists the result records it must produce and the statements of
what it does not cover (its anti-claims), and has a validator that checks it.
Until it has that executable contract, its prose can help a reader find their
way and has no authority over the system.
nodes.title: Make doctrine executable before authoritative

nodes.plain: Files Microcosm writes about itself get no exemptions. Its standards, paper modules, ledgers, routes, generated pages and release claims must meet the same evidence, anti-claim and refusal requirements they apply to everything else.

analogy.boundary: The calibration picture covers equal treatment only; it does not tell you whether the lab's instruments are accurate.

maps.analogy: the lab's own measuring instruments
maps.doctrine: the system's own documents about itself

maps.analogy: the calibration standard
maps.doctrine: the evidence, stated-limit and refusal rules

maps.analogy: the same standard applied to customers' equipment
maps.doctrine: the same rules applied to the work it audits

maps.analogy: no looser rule for the lab's own gauges
maps.doctrine: no exemption for the system's own documents

analogy.text: A calibration lab's own instruments must pass the same calibration check the lab applies to its customers' equipment, with no looser rule for its own gauges.

reader.counterexample: The system publishes a self-assessment calling its own work verified and complete, in wording that would fail the evidence rules it applies to the components it audits.
reader.does_not_prove: Meeting its own rules removes a double standard; it does not make the system complete or ready.

example.text: The release wording gate applies the same claim-language rules to the system's own public copy as to any other component, so overclaiming wording in a self-description is blocked at release.

reader.governs: Claims the system makes about itself.
reader.plain: When the system describes or assesses itself, that description has to meet exactly the same evidence and honesty standard it enforces on everything else.
reader.potential_misread: That a system describing itself can be taken at its word, or that meeting the standard makes its self-description correct.
reader.refuses: A lighter standard for the system's own documents than for the work they audit.
reader.requires: Holding standards, paper modules, ledgers, routes, generated pages and release wording to the same evidence, stated-limit and refusal rules as any other component.
reader.why_it_matters: A system's statements about itself are where overclaiming hides most easily, so holding them to the same rules keeps its public limits honest.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-12.
Obligation grounding: AX-12.O1.microcosm_claims_use_same_gate, AX-12.O2.release_claim_language_blocked, AX-12.O3.receipt_body_and_doctrine_overclaim_blocked, AX-12.O4.evidence_truth_floor_blocks_release.

Files Microcosm writes about itself get no exemptions. Its standards, paper
modules, ledgers, routes, generated pages and release claims must meet the same
evidence, anti-claim and refusal requirements they apply to everything else.
nodes.title: Apply the same floor to meta artifacts

nodes.plain: The content hash records which bytes or rows were used; the provenance label records where they may go and how strongly they may be claimed. A piece of data needs both before it is fully routed.

analogy.boundary: The two-tag picture covers only the need for both at once; a fully tagged sample can still be the wrong sample.

maps.analogy: the label naming the patient and the draw
maps.doctrine: the recorded inputs the value was built from

maps.analogy: the handling tag stating what the sample may be tested for
maps.doctrine: the origin class and usage limit

maps.analogy: a tube with only one tag is set aside
maps.doctrine: a value missing either record is not fully described

analogy.text: A blood sample needs a label saying which patient and which draw it came from, and a handling tag saying what it may be tested for. A tube with only one of the two is set aside.

reader.counterexample: A reused result record has a clean origin label and no content hash, so it keeps being trusted after the source it was built from has changed.
reader.does_not_prove: Carrying both records shows a value is fully described, and says nothing about whether the value is correct.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings public material in with a manifest and a hash for each file, so the imported copy carries both the hash that detects source changes and the origin label that limits where it may go.

reader.governs: Values that are reused or that cross from one part of the system to another.
reader.plain: Every piece of data needs two tags at once, one saying exactly which inputs it was built from and one saying where it may go and how strongly it can be claimed. If either tag is missing, the data is not ready to use.
reader.potential_misread: That one good label is enough, when knowing the source says nothing about where a value may travel and a usage tag means little without the inputs.
reader.refuses: Treating a value as fully described when it records only its inputs or only its origin.
reader.requires: A recorded input hash that forces a recompute when it no longer matches, and an origin class with a usage limit carried across every boundary, both on the same value.
reader.why_it_matters: Data cannot be trusted on half a paper trail, where you know what it is but not where it may go, or the reverse.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-4, AX-8.
Obligation grounding: AX-4.O1.content_basis_digest_declared, AX-4.O2.equal_basis_permits_reuse, AX-4.O3.digest_drift_forces_recompute, AX-4.O4.freshness_basis_mismatch_materialized, AX-8.O1.label_propagation, AX-8.O2.sink_policy, AX-8.O3.lying_endpoint_rejected.

The content hash records which bytes or rows were used; the provenance label
records where they may go and how strongly they may be claimed. A piece of data
needs both before it is fully routed.
nodes.title: Carry basis and provenance together

nodes.plain: Generated docs, markdown summaries, route cards and paper modules may present what the source says and may never raise it. When the source content, the grammar or the source's status no longer supports a generated page, recompute the page from the source or lower its status.

analogy.boundary: The photocopy covers only a copy ranking below its original; it leaves out that a generated page is limited by several source properties at once, such as freshness and origin.

maps.analogy: the signed original contract
maps.doctrine: the source

maps.analogy: the photocopy that can be read and cannot overrule the original
maps.doctrine: the generated page kept at or below its source

maps.analogy: the old copy stops counting once the original is amended
maps.doctrine: regenerate or downgrade when the source weakens

analogy.text: A photocopy of a contract can be read and shared, and the signed original still decides. When the original is amended, the old copy stops counting.

reader.counterexample: A polished summary page is cited as the authority for a number after the source it was generated from has changed.
reader.does_not_prove: Keeping a generated page below its source stops the page adding authority and does nothing to make the source correct.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings public material in with a manifest and a hash for each file, and the imported copy is never allowed to outrank the original it was copied from.

reader.governs: The relation between a source and the pages generated from it.
reader.plain: A generated page can display what a source says, but it carries no more authority than that source. If the source weakens, the page has to be regenerated or marked down.
reader.potential_misread: That a clear, confident-looking page must be reliable, when it can only be as reliable as its source.
reader.refuses: A generated page, card or summary that claims more than the source it summarizes.
reader.requires: Keeping a generated page at or below its source's support, freshness, origin and grammar check, and regenerating or downgrading it when any of those weakens.
reader.why_it_matters: A polished public page cannot be treated as more trustworthy than the source it was generated from.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-4, AX-5, AX-11.
Obligation grounding: AX-4.O1.content_basis_digest_declared, AX-4.O2.equal_basis_permits_reuse, AX-4.O3.digest_drift_forces_recompute, AX-4.O4.freshness_basis_mismatch_materialized, AX-5.O1.composite_status_meets_parts, AX-5.O2.no_evidence_defaults_blocked, AX-5.O3.authority_cannot_raise_without_derivation, AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection.

Generated docs, markdown summaries, route cards and paper modules may present
what the source says and may never raise it. When the source content, the
grammar or the source's status no longer supports a generated page, recompute
the page from the source or lower its status.
nodes.title: Keep projections below source authority

nodes.plain: Permission to change a file depends on more than who has access to it. It combines permission derived from a proof, the write scope claimed for this change, the current parent commit, a way to undo the change, and evidence that this particular transaction landed.

analogy.boundary: The transfer picture covers only several conditions holding together; it leaves out the declared write scope and the landing record the rule also requires.

maps.analogy: the bank checking this transfer against your approved limit, beyond your being a signatory
maps.doctrine: permission worked out from proof and policy, instead of standing access

maps.analogy: the account still showing the balance you expected
maps.doctrine: current parent state matching what was expected

maps.analogy: a reversal path if the transfer was wrong
maps.doctrine: a way to undo the effect

analogy.text: Being a signatory on a bank account does not send a transfer. It goes through only when the amount is within your approved limit, the account still shows the balance you expected, and there is a way to reverse it.

reader.counterexample: A write goes ahead because the agent already holds a token and can reach the file, landing on whatever the current head is, with no declared scope and no way to undo.
reader.does_not_prove: One write meeting all five conditions says nothing about other write paths in the system.

example.text: The proof-derived mutation authorization component allows a change only when permission comes from policy and proof references for that effect, and rejects a write that relies on a standing credential, so permission is worked out for each transaction.

reader.governs: Whether a write to a file or record may go ahead.
reader.plain: Permission to change something takes several conditions holding together for this exact change. You need worked-out permission, agreed limits on what you may touch, a current state that still matches what you expected, a way to undo, and a record that it landed.
reader.potential_misread: That having access means you may change something, when permission still has to be worked out for this exact change against the state you actually find.
reader.refuses: Treating reach or a standing credential as permission, or writing on whatever state exists without an expected parent, a scope or a way to undo.
reader.requires: Tying the write to this transaction through worked-out permission, a declared scope, the expected parent state, a way to undo it or a declared point of no return, and a landing record.
reader.why_it_matters: Someone with broad standing access cannot make a change that nothing has checked against its scope, the current state and a way to undo it.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-3, AX-9.
Obligation grounding: AX-3.O1.authorization_is_derived, AX-3.O2.standing_credential_insufficient, AX-3.O3.tool_effects_require_declared_scope, AX-9.O1.effect_boundary_declared, AX-9.O2.cas_parent_enforced, AX-9.O3.single_writer_claim_constraint.

Permission to change a file depends on more than who has access to it. It
combines permission derived from a proof, the write scope claimed for this
change, the current parent commit, a way to undo the change, and evidence that
this particular transaction landed.
nodes.title: Bind authority to transaction scope

nodes.plain: Before adding or removing a link between doctrine records in a registry where keys repeat, tie the change to the one source row, the target id and the builder that will read it. A generated page, a change in a count or a nearby key with the same name is no substitute for that row.

analogy.boundary: The booking picture covers tracing a connection to one exact entry; it does not tell you whether that entry is right.

maps.analogy: the exact scheduled service for that date and route
maps.doctrine: the unique source row that names the relation

maps.analogy: a similar flight number or one more listed service is no booking
maps.doctrine: a similar key or changed count is no substitute

maps.analogy: the specific booking the connecting seat belongs to
maps.doctrine: the target id and builder route the edge feeds

analogy.text: Before adding a connecting flight to a booking, the agent points to the exact scheduled service for that date and route. A similar flight number, or a timetable that now lists one more service, is no reason to book the seat.

reader.counterexample: A builder adds an edge because the generated registry now reports one more neighbour, without finding the source row that would justify it.
reader.does_not_prove: Pointing a change at its source row shows where the edge came from, and the edge can still be wrong.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings each relation in against a named manifest row and hash and writes it inside a declared boundary, so an edge is added only where a current source row names it.

reader.governs: Adding or removing an edge in a registry of similar-looking rows.
reader.plain: Before adding or removing a connection in a list of relationships, point to the exact source entry that names it and the place that will use it. A similar entry nearby, or a count that went up by one, is not enough.
reader.potential_misread: That a close match or a changed count confirms the connection, when only the exact entry naming the relationship does.
reader.refuses: Adding an edge because of a generated page, a changed count or a similar nearby key, without the row that owns it.
reader.requires: A unique source row with a recorded content hash, a change made against that row's expected parent state by one writer, and an edge that passes the grammar.
reader.why_it_matters: In a list where many entries look alike, acting on a near match wires up the wrong relationship, and the mistake is hard to find later.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-4, AX-9, AX-11.
Obligation grounding: AX-4.O1.content_basis_digest_declared, AX-4.O2.equal_basis_permits_reuse, AX-4.O3.digest_drift_forces_recompute, AX-4.O4.freshness_basis_mismatch_materialized, AX-9.O1.effect_boundary_declared, AX-9.O2.cas_parent_enforced, AX-9.O3.single_writer_claim_constraint, AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection.

Before adding or removing a link between doctrine records in a registry where
keys repeat, tie the change to the one source row, the target id and the builder
that will read it. A generated page, a change in a count or a nearby key with
the same name is no substitute for that row.
nodes.title: Anchor graph mutations to unique source rows

nodes.plain: A staged law, standard, component or generated page becomes active only when its owner boundary, source row, matching generated output, validation result record and status change have all landed in the same governed transaction, or when an explicit blocked result record records where the work stopped. If the source a page was generated from has uncommitted changes held by another active owner, the page is not yet current; ask for a handoff, wait for that owner to land the change, or write a bloc

analogy.boundary: The bylaw picture covers only all the steps landing together; it says nothing about whether the bylaw is wise, and it leaves out the case where a partial item is explicitly held in place.

maps.analogy: the bylaw voted, signed, registered and marked in force at one sitting
maps.doctrine: all required pieces landing in one transaction

maps.analogy: a tabled draft is still a proposal
maps.doctrine: a staged item is not yet active

maps.analogy: a draft that passed some steps and was never registered is held over
maps.doctrine: a partly landed change stays pending

analogy.text: A new bylaw takes effect only when it is voted in, signed, entered in the register and marked as in force at one sitting. A draft circulating in the room is still a proposal.

reader.counterexample: A generated card is treated as live the moment it renders, while its source is still being edited by another owner and has not landed.
reader.does_not_prove: This rule fixes when a change starts to count, and the change can still be wrong once it does.

example.text: The mission transaction spine lands a multi-step change as one sequence with a compare-and-swap on the parent and a single writer, so a staged item counts as active only after the whole transaction commits.

reader.governs: When a staged change may start counting as active.
reader.plain: A new rule does not start to count just because a draft has appeared. Its owner, exact source entry, matching generated copy, passing check and recorded status change all have to land together in one step, and until then it is pending.
reader.potential_misread: That once a draft looks complete it is in force, when it counts only after ownership, source, generated copy, check and status change land together.
reader.refuses: Treating a partly landed change, or a page generated from a source another owner is still editing, as active.
reader.requires: Owner, source row, matching generated copy, validation record and status change all landing in one single-writer transaction, or an explicit blocked record that keeps the change's place.
reader.why_it_matters: Nobody acts on a half-finished draft as if it were the live rule when some steps never happened.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-3, AX-9, AX-11, AX-12.
Obligation grounding: AX-3.O1.authorization_is_derived, AX-3.O2.standing_credential_insufficient, AX-3.O3.tool_effects_require_declared_scope, AX-9.O1.effect_boundary_declared, AX-9.O2.cas_parent_enforced, AX-9.O3.single_writer_claim_constraint, AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection, AX-12.O1.microcosm_claims_use_same_gate, AX-12.O2.release_claim_language_blocked, AX-12.O3.receipt_body_and_doctrine_overclaim_blocked, AX-12.O4.evidence_truth_floor_blocks_release.

A staged law, standard, component or generated page becomes active only when its
owner boundary, source row, matching generated output, validation result record
and status change have all landed in the same governed transaction, or when an
explicit blocked result record records where the work stopped. If the source a
page was generated from has uncommitted changes held by another active owner,
the page is not yet current; ask for a handoff, wait for that owner to land the
change, or write a blocked result record before treating the page as current.
Anything only partly admitted stays recorded as an open gap.
nodes.title: Require fan-in before activation

nodes.plain: A residual is a recorded, typed gap where a link might belong, and it is kept separate from the links themselves. Before wiring a missing neighbour, record the declared domain, the source row, whether the target resolves, whether the gap can be filled, the minimum evidence required, and the anti-claim. A candidate route, a neighbour suggested by generated output, a matching file name, a single match or a stale row in a generated page all remain gaps. A gap becomes a link only when the current so

analogy.boundary: The transit map covers only the need for a real service; it leaves out the typed record a gap keeps while it waits.

maps.analogy: a known gap on the map, marked and not yet drawn
maps.doctrine: the missing relation recorded as a typed gap

maps.analogy: the line drawn only when a scheduled service connects the stations
maps.doctrine: the edge added only when a source names it and the target exists

analogy.text: A transit map draws a line between two stations only when a real service runs between them, however close together they sit.

reader.counterexample: A builder adds an edge because two ids share a file name, turning a naming coincidence into a claimed relationship.
reader.does_not_prove: Classifying a gap keeps it from being faked, and the gap stays open until a source row names the relation.

example.text: The drift control room reports where a generated page has moved away from its source as a typed gap to recompute, and leaves the edge alone instead of rewriting it to make the card look complete.

reader.governs: When a gap in the map may be filled with an edge.
reader.plain: A missing link in the map is a recorded gap with a type, left open until filled properly. You draw the link only once a current source names it and the target really exists.
reader.potential_misread: That a plausible-looking connection is real, when closeness or a shared name is only a reason to check.
reader.refuses: Turning a guess, a matching file name or a generated hint into an edge, in either direction between doctrine and the system.
reader.requires: Classifying a missing neighbour as a typed gap with its declared area, source row, target and needed evidence before adding any edge.
reader.why_it_matters: The map stays accurate as it grows, with no invented connections added to make a diagram look complete.

nodes.statement:
Grounding: AX-5, AX-6, AX-11.
Obligation grounding: AX-5.O2.no_evidence_defaults_blocked, AX-5.O3.authority_cannot_raise_without_derivation, AX-6.O1.closed_world_domain_declared, AX-6.O2.absence_not_negation, AX-6.O3.fact_claims_cite_loci_and_dag, AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection.

A residual is a recorded, typed gap where a link might belong, and it is kept
separate from the links themselves. Before wiring a missing neighbour, record
the declared domain, the source row, whether the target resolves, whether the
gap can be filled, the minimum evidence required, and the anti-claim. A
candidate route, a neighbour suggested by generated output, a matching file
name, a single match or a stale row in a generated page all remain gaps. A gap
becomes a link only when the current source row names the relation and the
builder resolves the target. The same rule applies in both directions between
principles and the system's code: a link from a principle to the code must come
from a source row, and evidence from the code may narrow which ids a principle
governs only when current source rows name the relation. Neither kind of link
counts as support for the principle or gives a generated page authority, and
neither may be used to turn a gap into a link. If the code cannot name the
target from a source row, keep the gap open and record how to return to it;
never invent a relationship or mark the health card clean to hide the gap.
nodes.title: Classify residual pressure before wiring

nodes.plain: Generating a doctrine record's pages does not make the record active. Attach its validator result records, evidence references, omissions, anti-claims and authority limits to the record before treating its JSON, markdown, routing link or public copy as current and authoritative.

analogy.boundary: The medicine picture covers attaching records before use; it does not tell you whether the underlying tests were any good.

maps.analogy: attaching the test results before the medicine is cleared
maps.doctrine: attaching validator results before the record counts

maps.analogy: the list of what was tested and the known side effects on file
maps.doctrine: evidence references and stated omissions on the record

maps.analogy: the approved use that limits what the medicine may be sold for
maps.doctrine: the scope limit attached to the record

analogy.text: A medicine is cleared for sale once the test results, the list of what was tested, the known side effects and the approved use are all on file. A printed leaflet alone does not clear it.

reader.counterexample: A generated doctrine card is cited as current authority for a rule because the JSON exists and the heading sounds confident, with no validator results, omissions or scope limit attached.
reader.does_not_prove: Attaching results to a record limits what it may claim and does not make the record correct.

example.text: The release wording gate applies the same claim-language rules to the system's own doctrine copy as to any other component, so a record's public line cannot claim more than its attached checks support.

reader.governs: When a doctrine record may be used as current authority.
reader.plain: A record does not become the trusted version just because a readable copy exists. The results of its checks, references to its evidence, what it leaves out and how far it may claim all have to be attached first.
reader.potential_misread: That a clear, complete-looking record is authoritative, when authority comes only from the checks and limits attached to it.
reader.refuses: Treating a record's JSON, markdown, routing edge or public copy as authoritative because it exists.
reader.requires: Validator results, evidence references, omissions, stated limits and a scope limit attached to the record before any copy of it is treated as current authority.
reader.why_it_matters: A nicely formatted record cannot be treated as the trusted source when the checks and limits behind it were never attached.

Grounding: AX-11, AX-12.
Obligation grounding: AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection, AX-12.O1.microcosm_claims_use_same_gate, AX-12.O3.receipt_body_and_doctrine_overclaim_blocked, AX-12.O4.evidence_truth_floor_blocks_release.

Generating a doctrine record's pages does not make the record active. Attach its
validator result records, evidence references, omissions, anti-claims and
authority limits to the record before treating its JSON, markdown, routing link
or public copy as current and authoritative.
nodes.title: Bind receipts before record authority

nodes.plain: Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim or model answer without recomputing it from the lower-level evidence.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers repeating an old sign; it leaves out that the verdict has to be worked out again from the shelves themselves.

maps.analogy: yesterday's sign, repeated
maps.doctrine: the repeated verdict or label

maps.analogy: the look at the shelves that nobody did
maps.doctrine: the missing recomputation from the evidence

analogy.text: Seeing yesterday's 'sold out' sign in a shop window and telling people the shop is sold out today, without looking at whether the shelves were restocked overnight.

reader.counterexample: A dashboard shows a component as healthy because the component's own record says so, and nothing recomputes that verdict.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching repeated labels in these replays says nothing about whether any particular claim is true.

example.text: The scheming-monitor replay is given a trace with a deliberately wrong label, recomputes the verdict from the trace, and rejects the run, so the wrong label cannot pass by being repeated.

reader.governs: Any point where a written label could be used in place of a recomputed verdict.
reader.plain: The mistake of repeating a stored verdict, label or model answer as if it were true, without working it out again from the evidence it should rest on.
reader.potential_misread: That a label being present means someone checked it.
reader.refuses: Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, Markdown claim or model answer as if repetition made it true.
reader.requires: A verdict recomputed from the underlying evidence, and a test case with a wrong label that the recomputation rejects.
reader.why_it_matters: One unchecked label can be quoted as fact by every step that comes after it.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-1 Fixture-label echo | AX-1, AX-12 | Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim or model answer without recomputing it from the lower-level evidence. |
nodes.title: Fixture-label echo

nodes.plain: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential or past success where a checker, proof, policy or checked capability should decide.

analogy.boundary: The picture stops at the door; whether the access system itself is right, or how the person behaves inside, is beyond it.

maps.analogy: letting the person in because the face is familiar and the pass looks right
maps.doctrine: trusting a claim because of its producer or credential

maps.analogy: looking the person up in the access system for this room today
maps.doctrine: the independent checker or permission lookup that should decide

maps.analogy: the old pass that worked last time
maps.doctrine: a previous successful run or long-lived credential

analogy.text: A security guard waves someone into a secure room because he recognises their face and they hold an old pass, without looking them up in the access system to see whether they are cleared for that room today.

reader.counterexample: A change to files is allowed because the caller holds a long-lived credential and the same route passed last time, and nothing looks up whether the caller is allowed to make this change now.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing identity-based trust in these replays leaves open whether the permissions that are granted are correct.

example.text: The tool-authority replay works out whether a tool call is allowed from the capability and policy it looks up, so a known caller with no permission for that call is refused.

reader.governs: Decisions about whether to trust a claim or allow an action.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting something through because of who sent it, what badge it carries or that it worked last time, without checking that this request is allowed right now.
reader.potential_misread: That a trusted name, or a pass that worked before, is a safe substitute for checking this request.
reader.refuses: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential or past success in place of a checker, proof, policy or a permission looked up for this request.
reader.requires: A small checker that decides each certificate, and permission for each action worked out from current tokens, policy and proof references.
reader.why_it_matters: Identities can be faked or go out of date, and when that happens a system that trusts the sender has nothing checking the request.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-2 Producer trust | AX-2, AX-3 | Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential or past success where a checker, proof, policy or checked capability should decide. |
nodes.title: Producer trust

nodes.plain: Reading counts, handles, passing validators or evidence classes as a measure of product maturity, release readiness or whole-system correctness.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers hidden gaps in a tally; it says nothing about whether the lines that do report are running well.

maps.analogy: the forty on-time trains read as the whole network being fine
maps.doctrine: a count or tally read as the standing of the whole

maps.analogy: a line with no data on the board that could be closed
maps.doctrine: a part with no supporting evidence, which should hold the whole down

maps.analogy: the network being only as good as its worst line
maps.doctrine: the status of the whole being its weakest part

analogy.text: A station board says forty trains ran on time, and someone concludes the whole network is running well, although several lines have no data on the board and could be closed.

reader.counterexample: A progress page reports that ninety checks pass and calls the system ready for release, while several required parts have no supporting evidence and the gaps are averaged away.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing to read counts and passing validators as a maturity score adds no support to any part.

example.text: The coverage ledger counts how many declared parts actually exist and includes a test case that fails if a missing entry is read as covered, so its tally reports a bounded count.

reader.governs: Progress and readiness reports that summarise many parts with one number.
reader.plain: The mistake of reading one summary number, such as how many checks passed, as if it said the whole thing is finished or ready, when parts nobody measured could still be failing.
reader.potential_misread: That more passing checks always means more readiness, when repeating a check that already passed adds nothing.
reader.refuses: Treating counts, names, passing validators or evidence-class names as product maturity, release readiness or correctness of the whole system.
reader.requires: Scoring the whole by its weakest part, counting a part with no evidence as blocked, and raising standing only by new coverage, a higher score on a part or a missing negative case.
reader.why_it_matters: Counting passes as a maturity score treats everything unmeasured as passed, so a project can look ready for release while a required piece was never tested.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-3 Rank-as-product-score | AX-5, AX-12 | Reading counts, handles, passing validators or evidence classes as a measure of product maturity, release readiness or whole-system correctness. |
nodes.title: Rank-as-product-score

nodes.plain: Reusing a cached result looked up by name, path, route, display label or producer after the content it was computed from has changed.

analogy.boundary: The picture covers one card; finding one wrong card does not tell you whether the rest of the catalogue is current.

maps.analogy: the catalogue card filed under the title and shelf
maps.doctrine: a saved result kept under a name that does not change

maps.analogy: the book on the shelf, swapped for a different edition
maps.doctrine: the content behind the name, which has changed

maps.analogy: checking the book on the shelf before trusting the card
maps.doctrine: keying reuse on a hash of the content

analogy.text: A library catalogue card says a title is on shelf B, but the book there was swapped for a different edition and nobody updated the card.

reader.counterexample: A page keeps serving a number from an unchanged route long after someone edited the source the number was computed from.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching one stale reuse at one hash check leaves every other cache unexamined, and the source records freshness tracking across the system as still incomplete.

example.text: The source-import protocol keys each imported copy on a content hash and refuses to reuse the copy when the source hash no longer matches, so a changed source cannot be served from its old path.

reader.governs: Any reuse of a saved result.
reader.plain: The mistake of reusing a saved answer filed under a name or address after the thing behind that name has been changed or replaced.
reader.potential_misread: That an unchanged name means unchanged content.
reader.refuses: Serving a saved result by name, path, route, label or producer after the inputs it was computed from have changed.
reader.requires: A cache key computed from a hash of the inputs, with a recompute or a refusal when the hash no longer matches.
reader.why_it_matters: Pipelines reuse saved results by name to save time, and when the source has been edited the name keeps returning an out-of-date answer without anyone noticing.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-4 Cache-across-drift | AX-4, AX-10 | Reusing a cached result looked up by name, path, route, display label or producer after the content it was computed from has changed. |
nodes.title: Cache-across-drift

nodes.plain: Reading missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared domain in which every case was checked.

analogy.boundary: The picture only separates 'found nothing' from 'there is nothing'; it says nothing about whether the unimaged region is healthy.

maps.analogy: the region of the body that was never imaged
maps.doctrine: an obligation with no supporting evidence

maps.analogy: reporting the unimaged region as clear
maps.doctrine: reading that gap as a negative finding

maps.analogy: saying 'clear' only for the area that was actually scanned
maps.doctrine: recording a negative only inside a declared finite set of cases that were all checked

analogy.text: A doctor reports a region of a scan as clear when that region was never imaged, so 'we saw no problem' becomes 'there is no problem'.

reader.counterexample: A coverage map marks an area as clear because no failing case turned up there, although nobody declared or searched a finite set of cases for that area.
reader.does_not_prove: Recording a gap as unknown settles nothing about the missing claim in either direction.

example.text: The coverage ledger records each thing the system has not established as an open gap with a stated scope, and includes a test case that fails if a blank entry is read as a negative.

reader.governs: Coverage reports, wherever a missing result could be read as a negative finding.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating a place where nothing was found as a finding that nothing is there, when nobody may have looked, or looked everywhere.
reader.potential_misread: That a blank entry means a confirmed 'nothing here', when it only means nobody knows unless every case in a declared area was checked.
reader.refuses: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared finite set of cases.
reader.requires: Recording an uncovered obligation as an open gap, and recording a negative only inside a declared finite set of cases.
reader.why_it_matters: An unexamined gap reads as reassurance, so a coverage map can look complete while the risk sits exactly where nobody checked.

| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-5 Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness | AX-6 | Reading missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared domain in which every case was checked. |
nodes.title: Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness

nodes.plain: Returning a number or conclusion from a computation whose preconditions failed, where a typed refusal was required.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers the missing input; it says nothing about whether a dose worked out from complete inputs is right.

maps.analogy: the missing patient weight the dose formula needs
maps.doctrine: a precondition that does not hold

maps.analogy: guessing a dose and handing it over
maps.doctrine: returning a value anyway to keep going

maps.analogy: a written note saying 'dose not worked out: weight missing'
maps.doctrine: a typed refusal carrying its reason and evidence

analogy.text: A pharmacist guesses a dose when the patient's weight, the one input the formula needs, is missing, instead of saying the dose cannot be worked out yet.

reader.counterexample: A statistics routine returns a coefficient computed beyond its valid sample size, and a later summary reports it as a normal result because it arrived as a number.
reader.does_not_prove: A correct refusal in one place says nothing about whether the numbers this computation does return are right.

example.text: The finance forecast evaluation component returns a typed refusal when the forecast horizon reaches or exceeds the sample size, or when the statistics library it needs is unavailable, instead of reporting a number computed outside its valid range.

reader.governs: Computations that are only valid for some inputs.
reader.plain: The mistake of producing a number anyway when something the number depends on is missing, instead of saying 'I cannot answer this, and here is why'.
reader.potential_misread: That returning some number is more helpful than refusing, when a number produced from missing inputs is worse because it passes as usable.
reader.refuses: Returning a meaningless statistic, a silent NaN or a conclusion outside the valid range just to keep the pipeline passing.
reader.requires: A result type that returns Ok only when the declared precondition holds and otherwise a refusal carrying the reason and evidence.
reader.why_it_matters: A made-up number looks like a real one to every later step, while a refusal stops the bad value where it starts.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-6 Inadmissible number emission | AX-7 | Returning a number or conclusion from a computation whose preconditions failed, where a typed refusal was required. |
nodes.title: Inadmissible number emission

nodes.plain: Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public destination without an origin label and a sanitizing transform.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers one border post; clearing goods there does not make every other border crossing safe.

maps.analogy: the goods arriving at the border
maps.doctrine: the private or untrusted value entering a pipeline

maps.analogy: entry into the country past customs
maps.doctrine: the public or high-trust destination

maps.analogy: the declaration form saying where the goods came from
maps.doctrine: the provenance label that has to travel with the value

maps.analogy: the inspection that clears the goods
maps.doctrine: the declared cleaning step the value has to pass through

maps.analogy: the ordinary truck that everyone waves through
maps.doctrine: the clean-looking final step that hides the leak

analogy.text: A customs officer waves a shipment through because the truck looks ordinary, although no declaration form came with the goods and nobody inspected them.

reader.counterexample: A public page prints a value copied from near a private source because the final copy step looked clean, with no provenance label carried through the copy and no cleaning step between the source and the page.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching leaks at the named endpoints leaves open whether labels are carried along every path in the system.

example.text: The prompt-injection replay attaches an information-flow policy to the data, so an untrusted instruction that reaches a tool call is caught there, even though it arrived through a trusted endpoint.

reader.governs: Every point where material passes into a public page or a privileged operation.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting private or untrusted material reach a public or high-trust place because the last step looked clean, without a label saying where it came from and without running it through a stated cleaning step.
reader.potential_misread: That material is safe to publish if the last copy step looks tidy and nothing obviously private is visible.
reader.refuses: Untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential or raw spoken material reaching a public or privileged destination with no provenance label and no declared transform.
reader.requires: A provenance label and claim limit that travel with each value, and a declared transform, allowed by the destination's policy, for any untrusted material.
reader.why_it_matters: It is how a system can publish material that sits next to private sources without leaking secrets, credentials or planted instructions onto a public page.

| AP-7 Public/private membrane breach | AX-8 | Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public destination without an origin label and a sanitizing transform. |
nodes.title: Public/private membrane breach

nodes.plain: Making an irreversible change without an undo step, a rollback record, a compare-and-swap or world-version guard, or an explicit declaration that it cannot be undone.

analogy.boundary: The picture covers only one transfer; setting up a recall and a balance check for it does nothing for the bank's other payments.

maps.analogy: the money leaving your account
maps.doctrine: the irreversible change being written

maps.analogy: either a recall option or a note in advance that this transfer cannot be reversed
maps.doctrine: an undo step or a declared point of no return

maps.analogy: checking the balance still matches what you saw before you send
maps.doctrine: the compare-and-swap check against the expected parent state

maps.analogy: two people moving money out of the same account at once
maps.doctrine: two writers racing on the same path

analogy.text: Sending a bank transfer that cannot be recalled without first checking that the balance has not changed since you last looked.

reader.counterexample: A step writes straight over a shared path assuming the previous state still holds, with no compare-and-swap and no undo, and silently overwrites another writer's change.
reader.does_not_prove: These safeguards cover the named landing paths and leave every other write in the system as it was.

example.text: The work-landing replay refuses to continue when the expected parent commit has moved or the head was not advanced as recorded, so a multi-step change cannot land on top of a state that has already changed.

reader.governs: Every change written to shared state.
reader.plain: The mistake of making a real change that is hard to undo while assuming it can be undone, when nothing was set up to undo it and nothing checked that the situation had not already moved.
reader.potential_misread: That because the normal case works, any change can be undone later if something goes wrong.
reader.refuses: Writing an irreversible change with no undo step, no rollback record, no compare-and-swap or version check, and no declared point of no return.
reader.requires: Either a way to undo the change or a declared point of no return, a compare-and-swap against the expected parent for multi-step changes, and one writer per path.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a change from silently overwriting someone else's work or stopping halfway with no record of how to undo it.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-8 Blind irreversible mutation | AX-9 | Making an irreversible change without an undo step, a rollback record, a compare-and-swap or world-version guard, or an explicit declaration that it cannot be undone. |
nodes.title: Blind irreversible mutation

nodes.plain: Writing a live fact into prose without its `as_of` date, the inputs it came from and a way to recompute it.

analogy.boundary: The picture only shows that painted text falls out of date; it says nothing about whether the live board itself is right.

maps.analogy: the train's departure time, which keeps changing
maps.doctrine: the changing value (a count or current state)

maps.analogy: painting it onto a permanent sign
maps.doctrine: writing it into permanent text

maps.analogy: a note saying when this time was correct
maps.doctrine: the date that should travel with it

maps.analogy: the timetable the departure time came from
maps.doctrine: the source it was read from

maps.analogy: the live board you could check for the current time
maps.doctrine: the route for recomputing it

analogy.text: Painting a train's departure time onto a permanent sign instead of showing it on the live board, so the sign keeps the old time after the timetable changes.

reader.counterexample: A page says "the system has 77 components" as a plain fact; the number was right when typed, but nothing records when it was read or how to recompute it, so it still reads as current long after it changed.
reader.does_not_prove: Blocking undated figures leaves open whether the dated ones are still current.

example.text: The fact-claim audit blocks a changing count that was written without a date, source and recompute route, so the figure is not accepted as fact just because it was once true.

reader.governs: Any changing value written into lasting text.
reader.plain: The mistake of writing a changing number or a 'current' status into permanent text as if it were fixed, with no note of when it was read, where it came from or how to work it out again.
reader.potential_misread: That a number true when it was written down stays a reliable fact afterwards.
reader.refuses: Writing a count, a 'current' state or a live total into text with no date, source or way to recompute it.
reader.requires: A date, a named source and a way to recompute the value, or else keeping it out of permanent text or labelling it a dated snapshot.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps readers from trusting an out-of-date figure that looks exactly like a current one.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-9 Frozen live fact | AX-10 | Writing a live fact into prose without its `as_of` date, the inputs it came from and a way to recompute it. |
nodes.title: Frozen live fact

nodes.plain: Giving doctrine prose the authority of an executable rule before it passes the grammar and lists the result records it must produce.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers notes that were never registered; a registered pass can still be wrong.

maps.analogy: the handwritten note on the door
maps.doctrine: the written doctrine claiming to govern

maps.analogy: being registered in the building's access system
maps.doctrine: being accepted by the executable grammar

maps.analogy: saying what evidence of access has to be shown
maps.doctrine: the record obligations it has to declare

maps.analogy: naming the rooms and hours the pass leaves out
maps.doctrine: the stated limits of its scope

analogy.text: Treating a handwritten note taped to a door, saying 'this person may enter', as real access, although it was never entered into the building's access system and never says which rooms or hours it covers.

reader.counterexample: A confidently worded policy paragraph is cited as the rule for some behaviour, although nothing parses or checks it and it never says what it leaves out.
reader.does_not_prove: A standard that passes the grammar is still only as strong as the obligations it carries.

example.text: The executable doctrine grammar accepts a standard as binding only when it parses and carries its obligation and scope-limit fields, and its tests include a written-only standard that claims to be complete, which the grammar rejects.

reader.governs: The line between rules that are enforced and text that only reads like a rule.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating a confidently written paragraph as a binding rule when it never went through the system's formal checks and never says what evidence it owes or where it applies.
reader.potential_misread: That a clearly and firmly worded statement is a rule the system enforces because of how it reads.
reader.refuses: Giving binding force to written doctrine that the grammar has not accepted and that declares no record obligations or scope limits.
reader.requires: Grammar acceptance plus declared record obligations and scope limits before a piece of doctrine counts as binding.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps confident paragraphs from piling up and being treated as enforced rules that nothing can check.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-10 Prose-as-executable-authority | AX-11 | Giving doctrine prose the authority of an executable rule before it passes the grammar and lists the result records it must produce. |
nodes.title: Prose-as-executable-authority

nodes.plain: Exempting Microcosm's own result records, docs, releases, generated pages or validators from the evidence checks Microcosm applies to everything else.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers who gets tested; passing the test still leaves open whether a sample is clean.

maps.analogy: the lab's own internal samples
maps.doctrine: the system's own pages, checkers, records and generated summaries

maps.analogy: the test run on every outside sample
maps.doctrine: the evidence rules it applies to outside claims

maps.analogy: passing the internal sample on the lab's word
maps.doctrine: accepting a claim about itself without those rules

maps.analogy: the lab's own quality check having to be tested too
maps.doctrine: the support evaluator that has to meet the standard it computes

analogy.text: A testing lab strictly retests every sample sent in from outside but passes its own internal samples on its own say-so.

reader.counterexample: A generated page reports the system as verified and complete because its own coverage summary said so, and nothing tests that statement against the rules applied to outside work.
reader.does_not_prove: Closing the exception removes special treatment and leaves open whether the system meets its own rules everywhere.

example.text: The release wording check applies the same claim-language rules to the system's own public text as to any other source, and blocks overclaiming lines in the system's own pages.

reader.governs: Claims the system makes about itself.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting the system's own pages, checkers, result records or generated views skip the evidence test it makes everything else pass, because it is the system talking about itself.
reader.potential_misread: That a claim is more trustworthy, and needs a lighter check, because the system is reporting on itself.
reader.refuses: A self-assessment of verified, complete or ready for release that would fail the rules the system applies to the work it audits.
reader.requires: The same evidence and refusal rules for every claim the system makes about itself, in pages, validators, result records and generated summaries.
reader.why_it_matters: It lets the system state its own limits plainly, without a flattering self-assessment slipping through as a new unchecked claim.

| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-11 Meta-artifact exemption | AX-12 | Exempting Microcosm's own result records, docs, releases, generated pages or validators from the evidence checks Microcosm applies to everything else. |
nodes.title: Meta-artifact exemption

nodes.plain: Using synthetic fixtures in place of real material that is available and safe to publish.

analogy.boundary: The picture only covers passing off a dummy as the real sample; dummy bags still have their use in training.

maps.analogy: the dummy blood bag
maps.doctrine: the synthetic fixture standing in for real material
